name: default
description: Industry-leading API style guide optimized for SDK generation (ogen, openapi-generator). Synthesized from Stripe, GitHub, Microsoft, and Zalando patterns. Enforces discriminated unions, named schemas, explicit nullability, and consistent operationIds for clean generated code.

designPrinciples.title: API First
designPrinciples.description: Design and document APIs before implementation. The OpenAPI specification is the contract between teams.

designPrinciples.title: Consumer-Centric Design
designPrinciples.description: Design APIs from the consumer's perspective. Optimize for the common use cases, not internal implementation.

designPrinciples.title: Consistency Over Cleverness
designPrinciples.description: Consistent patterns across endpoints reduce cognitive load. Predictable APIs are easier to learn and use.

designPrinciples.title: Design for Evolution
designPrinciples.description: APIs will change. Design for backward compatibility from day one. Never break existing clients.

designPrinciples.title: Simplicity
designPrinciples.description: Keep APIs simple. Avoid unnecessary complexity. When in doubt, leave it out.

designPrinciples.title: Self-Descriptive
designPrinciples.description: APIs should be discoverable and self-documenting. Good naming reduces the need for documentation.

categories.title: Naming Conventions
categories.description: Consistent naming for resources, properties, and URLs

categories.title: HTTP Methods
categories.description: Proper use of HTTP verbs and semantics

categories.title: Error Handling
categories.description: Consistent error responses using RFC 9457 Problem Details

categories.title: JSON Conventions
categories.description: JSON formatting and data type conventions

patterns.name: Cursor-Based Pagination
patterns.summary: Paginate large collections using opaque cursors for stable traversal
patterns.problem: Offset-based pagination breaks when items are added/removed during traversal. Large offsets cause performance issues.
patterns.solution: Use an opaque cursor (typically base64-encoded) that encodes the position in the result set. Return nextPageToken when more results exist.
patterns.when: Use for any collection endpoint that may return many items (>100). Especially important for real-time data that changes frequently.

examples.title: Cursor-based list response
examples.description: Client passes nextPageToken as pageToken query parameter to fetch next page

examples.title: List endpoint with pagination parameters
examples.description: pageSize controls items per page, pageToken continues from previous response

patterns.name: RFC 9457 Problem Details
patterns.summary: Return structured error responses following RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs
patterns.problem: Inconsistent error formats make it difficult for clients to handle errors programmatically and provide good user feedback.
patterns.solution: Return errors as application/problem+json with type (URI), title (human-readable), status (HTTP code), detail (specific message), and instance (occurrence URI).
patterns.when: Use for all 4xx and 5xx error responses. The format is extensible for domain-specific error fields.

examples.title: Validation error response
examples.code:
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/validation-error",
  "title": "Validation Failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "The email field must be a valid email address",
  "instance": "/v1/users/create/abc123"
}
examples.description: Machine-readable type URI, human-readable title and detail, HTTP status, and unique instance identifier

references.title: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

patterns.name: Standard CRUD Operations
patterns.summary: Map CRUD operations to HTTP methods consistently: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PATCH, Delete=DELETE
patterns.problem: Inconsistent HTTP method usage confuses clients and breaks REST semantics.
patterns.solution: Use POST for create (201), GET for read (200), PATCH for partial update (200), PUT for full replace (200), DELETE for remove (204).
patterns.when: Apply to all resource-oriented endpoints. Use POST for non-CRUD actions on sub-resources.

examples.title: User resource CRUD
examples.code:
POST   /v1/users         → 201 Created
GET    /v1/users/{id}    → 200 OK
PATCH  /v1/users/{id}    → 200 OK
DELETE /v1/users/{id}    → 204 No Content
examples.description: Consistent HTTP methods with appropriate status codes

patterns.name: Resource Naming
patterns.summary: Use plural nouns for collections, singular path parameters for items, kebab-case for paths
patterns.problem: Inconsistent naming creates confusion and makes APIs harder to learn.
patterns.solution: Collections use plural nouns (users, orders). Path parameters use kebab-case ({user-id}). Property names use camelCase.
patterns.when: Apply to all URL paths and JSON property names.

examples.title: Resource URL patterns
examples.description: Plural collections, kebab-case path parameters, hierarchical nesting

examples.title: Inconsistent naming
examples.description: Mixing singular/plural and different case conventions

patterns.name: Collection Response Envelope
patterns.summary: Wrap collection items in an envelope with pagination metadata
patterns.problem: Returning bare arrays prevents adding pagination metadata and other collection-level fields.
patterns.solution: Return an object with items array, nextPageToken (if more pages), and optionally totalCount.
patterns.when: Use for all list/collection endpoints. Even if pagination isn't needed now, the envelope allows adding it later.

examples.title: Collection response
examples.description: Items array with pagination token and optional total count

examples.title: Bare array response
examples.description: Cannot add pagination or collection metadata later without breaking change

patterns.name: Discriminated Unions
patterns.summary: Use a type discriminator field for polymorphic schemas to enable clean SDK code generation
patterns.problem: SDK generators cannot produce clean type-safe code for oneOf/anyOf without a discriminator. Clients must check multiple fields to determine the variant.
patterns.solution: Add a discriminator with propertyName (e.g., 'type') and mapping from values to schema refs.
patterns.when: Use whenever a field can be one of several types, especially for event payloads, notification types, or polymorphic resources.

examples.title: Discriminated payment method
examples.code:
PaymentMethod:
  oneOf:
    - $ref: '#/components/schemas/CreditCard'
    - $ref: '#/components/schemas/BankTransfer'
  discriminator:
    propertyName: type
    mapping:
      credit_card: '#/components/schemas/CreditCard'
      bank_transfer: '#/components/schemas/BankTransfer'
examples.description: Clear discriminator enables SDK to generate type-safe switch/match

patterns.name: Idempotency Keys
patterns.summary: Support idempotent retries for state-changing operations using client-provided idempotency keys
patterns.problem: Network failures can cause duplicate operations when clients retry. Without idempotency, a payment could be charged twice.
patterns.solution: Accept Idempotency-Key header on POST/PATCH operations. Store the key with request hash and return cached response on duplicate.
patterns.when: Essential for financial operations, resource creation, and any operation that cannot be safely repeated.

examples.title: Idempotent payment request
examples.description: Client provides UUID, server returns same response for duplicate keys

patterns.name: Long-Running Operations
patterns.summary: Return 202 Accepted for operations that take too long to complete synchronously
patterns.problem: Long operations cause timeouts and poor user experience if handled synchronously.
patterns.solution: Return 202 Accepted with Location header pointing to status endpoint. Status endpoint returns progress until complete, then redirects to result.
patterns.when: Use when operation typically takes >5 seconds. Examples: video processing, bulk imports, report generation.

examples.title: Async operation initiation
examples.description: Returns immediately with operation ID for polling

examples.title: Operation status response
examples.code:
GET /v1/operations/op-123

→ 200 OK
{"status": "completed", "result": {"reportUrl": "..."}}

or

→ 303 See Other
Location: /v1/reports/rpt-456
examples.description: Poll until completed, optionally redirect to result

rules.title: Provide OpenAPI 3.1 specification
rules.description: All APIs MUST have an OpenAPI 3.1 specification. The spec is the source of truth and MUST be maintained alongside code.
rules.rationale: OpenAPI enables tooling, documentation generation, client SDK generation, and contract testing. Version 3.1 aligns with JSON Schema draft 2020-12.

judge.prompt: Check if the OpenAPI specification uses version 3.1.x
passCriteria: openapi field is present at root

generate.prompt: Always start with openapi: 3.1.0 at the root of the specification
checklist: Include info section with title and version

rules.title: Use camelCase for property names
rules.description: All JSON property names MUST use camelCase (e.g., firstName, createdAt, userId).
rules.rationale: camelCase is native to JavaScript/JSON and aligns with OpenAPI conventions. It is the standard for Google, Microsoft, and GitHub APIs, and matches the PlexusOne codebase.
rules.source: Microsoft REST Guidelines, Google JSON Style Guide

judge.prompt: Check if all JSON property names use camelCase
passCriteria: All properties use camelCase (e.g., firstName, createdAt)
No underscores or hyphens in property names

generate.prompt: Use camelCase for all JSON property names (firstName, lastName, createdAt)
checklist: Use camelCase for all schema property names

rules.title: Use kebab-case for URL paths
rules.description: URL path segments MUST use kebab-case (lowercase with hyphens).
rules.rationale: Kebab-case is the standard for URLs. It's readable and avoids issues with case sensitivity in different systems.

judge.prompt: Check if all URL path segments use kebab-case (lowercase with hyphens)
passCriteria: Path parameters use camelCase in braces

generate.prompt: Use kebab-case for URL path segments (e.g., /user-accounts, /order-items)
checklist: Path parameters in camelCase within braces

rules.title: Use plural nouns for collection resources
rules.description: Collection resource names MUST be plural nouns. Use /users not /user, /orders not /order.
rules.rationale: Plural nouns make it clear you're dealing with a collection. GET /users returns multiple users, POST /users creates one user in the collection.

judge.prompt: Check if collection resource endpoints use plural nouns
passCriteria: All collection paths use plural nouns (users, orders, products)

generate.prompt: Use plural nouns for collection endpoints (e.g., /users, /orders, /products)

rules.title: Version APIs with URI prefix
rules.description: APIs MUST be versioned using a URI prefix: /v1/, /v2/, etc. Major version only.
rules.rationale: URI versioning is simple, explicit, and cacheable. Including version in the URL makes it obvious which version a client is using. Only major versions need to be in the URL since minor/patch changes are backward compatible.

judge.prompt: Check if API uses URI versioning with /v1/, /v2/ prefix pattern
passCriteria: All paths start with version prefix like /v1/

generate.prompt: Start all paths with version prefix /v1/ (major version only)
checklist: Use major version only (v1, v2, not v1.1)
Do not use query parameters or headers for versioning

rules.title: Use RFC 9457 Problem Details for errors
rules.description: Error responses MUST use the RFC 9457 Problem Details format with Content-Type: application/problem+json. RFC 9457 obsoletes RFC 9457 and adds the IANA Problem Type Registry.
rules.rationale: RFC 9457 is the IETF standard for HTTP API error responses (obsoletes RFC 9457). It provides a consistent structure with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields that clients can parse programmatically. The Problem Type Registry enables reuse of common error types across APIs.

good: {"type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-funds", "title": "Insufficient Funds", "status": 422, "detail": "Account balance is $10.00, but transaction requires $25.00", "instance": "/accounts/12345/transactions/67890"}

enforcement.reason: JSONPath filter expressions not supported by parser

judge.prompt: Check if error responses use RFC 9457 Problem Details format
passCriteria: Error schema has type, title, status, detail fields
Type URIs are meaningful (not about:blank for custom errors)
failCriteria: Custom error format without Problem Details fields

rules.title: Use cursor-based pagination
rules.description: Collection endpoints SHOULD use cursor-based pagination with `cursor` and `limit` parameters, returning `nextCursor` in the response.
rules.rationale: Cursor-based pagination is more scalable than offset-based. It handles real-time data changes gracefully and performs well on large datasets.

judge.prompt: Check if collection endpoints use cursor-based pagination

rules.title: Use standard HTTP methods correctly
rules.description: Use HTTP methods according to their semantics: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove).
rules.rationale: Correct HTTP method usage enables caching, idempotency guarantees, and predictable behavior.
rules.source: Zalando Z-148, Microsoft MS-030, PayPal PP-020

judge.prompt: Verify HTTP methods are used according to REST semantics
failCriteria: Actions in URL with wrong method

rules.title: GET and DELETE must be idempotent
rules.description: GET, PUT, and DELETE operations MUST be idempotent. Multiple identical requests must have the same effect as a single request.
rules.rationale: Idempotency enables safe retries and improves reliability. Clients can retry failed requests without causing duplicate operations.

judge.prompt: Check if GET, PUT, DELETE operations are idempotent

bad: DELETE /users/123 throws error on second call

rules.title: Return 201 Created with Location header for POST
rules.description: Successful POST requests that create resources MUST return 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource.
rules.rationale: 201 explicitly indicates creation. The Location header enables clients to fetch the created resource without parsing the response body.

judge.prompt: Check if POST endpoints return 201 Created with Location header for resource creation

rules.title: Use 204 No Content for successful DELETE
rules.description: Successful DELETE requests SHOULD return 204 No Content with an empty body.
rules.rationale: The resource no longer exists, so there's nothing to return. 204 clearly indicates success without a body.

judge.prompt: Check if DELETE endpoints return 204 No Content for successful deletion

good: HTTP/1.1 200 OK with deleted resource body

rules.title: Use 400 Bad Request for validation errors
rules.description: Use 400 Bad Request for client errors: malformed syntax, invalid parameters, validation failures.
rules.rationale: 400 is the generic client error. It tells the client the request was wrong and should not be retried without modification.

judge.prompt: Check if 400 Bad Request is documented for validation errors
passCriteria: 400 response defined for endpoints accepting input

good: 400 response with RFC 9457 body explaining invalid field

rules.title: Use 401 Unauthorized for missing/invalid authentication
rules.description: Use 401 Unauthorized when authentication is required but not provided or invalid.
rules.rationale: 401 specifically indicates an authentication problem. The client should authenticate and retry.

judge.prompt: Check if 401 Unauthorized is documented for authentication failures

rules.title: Use 403 Forbidden for authorization failures
rules.description: Use 403 Forbidden when the user is authenticated but not authorized to perform the action.
rules.rationale: 403 distinguishes authorization from authentication. The user is known but not permitted.

judge.prompt: Check if 403 Forbidden is documented for authorization failures
passCriteria: 403 response defined for endpoints with authorization

rules.title: Use 404 Not Found for missing resources
rules.description: Use 404 Not Found when the requested resource does not exist.
rules.rationale: 404 is clear and well-understood. Don't use 200 with an empty body or error message.

judge.prompt: Check if 404 Not Found is documented for missing resources
passCriteria: 404 response defined for endpoints with path parameters
failCriteria: Returns 200 with null for missing resources

bad: 200 OK with null body for missing resource

rules.title: Use 409 Conflict for state conflicts
rules.description: Use 409 Conflict when the request conflicts with current resource state (e.g., duplicate creation, invalid state transition).
rules.rationale: 409 indicates a conflict that the client might resolve. Useful for optimistic locking and state machines.

judge.prompt: Check if 409 Conflict is documented for state conflicts
failCriteria: No 409 for endpoints with unique constraints

rules.title: Use 422 Unprocessable Entity for semantic errors
rules.description: Use 422 Unprocessable Entity when the request is syntactically correct but semantically invalid (business rule violations).
rules.rationale: 422 distinguishes semantic errors from syntax errors (400). The request was understood but cannot be processed.

judge.prompt: Check if 422 Unprocessable Entity is documented for semantic errors
passCriteria: 422 response defined for business rule violations

good: 422 Unprocessable Entity for business rule violation

rules.title: Use 429 Too Many Requests for rate limiting
rules.description: Use 429 Too Many Requests when rate limiting is applied. Include Retry-After header.
rules.rationale: 429 tells clients they're being throttled. Retry-After helps them back off appropriately.

judge.prompt: Check if 429 Too Many Requests is documented for rate limiting

rules.title: Never expose internal errors to clients
rules.description: 5xx responses MUST NOT expose internal details (stack traces, database errors, internal paths). Use generic messages.
rules.rationale: Internal details are security risks and not useful to clients. Log details server-side, return generic messages to clients.

judge.prompt: Check that error schemas don't expose internal implementation details

good: 500 Internal Server Error with generic message and request ID
bad: 500 with stack trace or SQL error details

rules.title: Use ISO 8601 for dates and times
rules.description: All date and time values MUST use ISO 8601 format: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ssZ for timestamps, YYYY-MM-DD for dates.
rules.rationale: ISO 8601 is unambiguous and sortable. Always use UTC (Z suffix) for timestamps to avoid timezone confusion.

enforcement.reason: JSONPath filter expressions not supported by parser

judge.prompt: Check if date/time properties use ISO 8601 format
failCriteria: No format specified for date fields

rules.title: Use string for IDs
rules.description: Resource identifiers MUST be strings, not integers. Use UUIDs or prefixed IDs (e.g., userAbc123).
rules.rationale: String IDs are more flexible than integers. They support UUIDs, prefixed IDs, and don't have integer overflow issues. Prefixed IDs (userAbc123) are self-documenting.

judge.prompt: Check if resource identifiers use string type
passCriteria: All ID properties are type: string
Path parameters for IDs are strings
No integer IDs that could overflow

rules.title: Use Bearer token authentication
rules.description: Collection endpoints SHOULD use cursor-based pagination with `cursor` and `limit` parameters, returning `nextCursor` in the response.
rules.rationale: Bearer tokens are the standard for API authentication. They work with OAuth 2.0, JWT, and API keys.
rules.source: Zalando Z-220, Microsoft MS-100, PayPal PP-060

judge.prompt: Check if API uses Bearer token authentication
passCriteria: Security scheme uses http bearer or oauth2

rules.title: Document security requirements per endpoint
rules.description: Every endpoint MUST document its security requirements in the OpenAPI spec.
rules.rationale: Explicit security documentation prevents accidental exposure and enables security testing.

judge.prompt: Check if security requirements are documented per endpoint
failCriteria: Only global security defined without overrides

bad: No security defined on protected endpoints

rules.title: Support CORS for browser clients
rules.description: APIs consumed by browsers SHOULD support CORS with appropriate Access-Control-Allow-* headers.
rules.rationale: CORS enables secure cross-origin requests from web applications.

judge.prompt: Check if the API documents CORS support
partialCriteria: CORS mentioned but not fully documented

bad: No CORS documentation for browser API

rules.title: Include request ID in responses
rules.description: All responses SHOULD include a unique request ID header (X-Request-ID) for tracing and debugging.
rules.rationale: Request IDs enable correlation between client and server logs, essential for debugging distributed systems.

judge.prompt: Check if responses include request ID header for tracing

rules.title: Use standard filtering syntax
rules.description: Use query parameters for filtering: ?status=active&created_after=2024-01-01. Avoid complex query languages.
rules.rationale: Simple query parameters are easy to understand and implement. Complex filters can use POST with a body.

judge.prompt: Check if filtering uses simple query parameters

rules.title: Use sort parameter with field and direction
rules.description: Use ?sort=field or ?sort=-field for sorting. Prefix with - for descending order.
rules.rationale: This pattern is common and concise. Multiple fields can be comma-separated: ?sort=-createdAt,name

judge.prompt: Check if sorting uses ?sort=field or ?sort=-field pattern

rules.title: Document all endpoints with summary and description
rules.description: Every endpoint MUST have a summary (one line) and description (detailed explanation) in the OpenAPI spec.
rules.rationale: Good documentation reduces support burden and improves developer experience. Summary appears in tooling, description provides detail.

judge.prompt: Check if all endpoints have summary and description

good: summary: Create a new user\ndescription: Creates a user account with the provided details...

rules.title: Provide examples for all schemas
rules.description: All request/response schemas SHOULD include realistic examples.
rules.rationale: Examples help developers understand expected data formats. They're used in documentation and testing.

judge.prompt: Check if schemas include realistic examples

good:
example:
  id: user_abc123
  email: alice@example.com

rules.title: Deprecate before removing
rules.description: Endpoints MUST be deprecated for at least 6 months before removal. Use Sunset header to communicate removal date.
rules.rationale: Graceful deprecation gives clients time to migrate. Sudden removal breaks integrations.

judge.prompt: Check if deprecated endpoints have Sunset headers and sufficient notice period

rules.title: Never remove fields, only add
rules.description: Collection responses MUST use a consistent envelope: {"items": [...], "nextCursor": "...", "hasMore": true}
rules.rationale: Removing fields breaks existing clients. Add new fields and deprecate old ones if needed.

rules.title: Use ETag for caching and concurrency
rules.description: GET responses SHOULD include ETag header. PUT/PATCH SHOULD support If-Match for optimistic locking.
rules.rationale: ETags enable efficient caching and prevent lost updates in concurrent modifications.

judge.prompt: Check if ETag headers are used for caching and concurrency
partialCriteria: Only ETag or only If-Match present

rules.title: Limit response size
rules.description: Collection endpoints MUST limit response size. Default to 20-50 items, max 100.
rules.rationale: Unbounded responses cause performance issues and timeout errors. Always paginate.

judge.prompt: Check if collection endpoints have reasonable size limits

rules.title: Use consistent envelope for collections
rules.description: Collection responses MUST use a consistent envelope: {"items": [...], "nextCursor": "...", "hasMore": true}
rules.rationale: A consistent envelope enables generic client handling and clearly separates data from metadata.

rules.title: Support partial responses with fields parameter
rules.description: Endpoints MAY support ?fields=id,name,email to return only specified fields.
rules.rationale: Partial responses reduce bandwidth and improve performance for mobile clients.

rules.title: Use HTTPS only
rules.description: All API endpoints MUST be served over HTTPS. HTTP MUST redirect to HTTPS or return 400.
rules.rationale: HTTPS protects data in transit. There's no reason to use HTTP for production APIs.

rules.title: Document rate limits

rules.title: Use PATCH for partial updates
rules.description: Use PATCH (not PUT) for partial resource updates. Only send changed fields.
rules.rationale: PATCH is designed for partial updates. PUT replaces the entire resource and requires the client to send all fields.

rules.title: Return created/updated resource in response
rules.description: POST and PATCH SHOULD return the created/updated resource in the response body.
rules.rationale: Returning the resource saves a round-trip GET and shows server-computed fields (id, timestamps).

rules.title: Require operationId for all operations

bad: Returns all 10000 items in single response

rules.title: Include self link
rules.description: Resources MAY include a 'self' link for discoverability.
rules.rationale: Self links enable clients to refresh resources and support HATEOAS patterns.

judge.prompt: Check if resources include self links for discoverability

rules.title: Use standard link relations
rules.description: Use IANA standard link relations when available (self, next, prev, first, last).
rules.rationale: Standard relations are widely understood and enable generic client handling.

judge.prompt: Check if link relations use IANA standard names
passCriteria: Uses standard relations: self, next, prev, first, last

rules.title: Support batch operations
rules.description: Consider supporting batch endpoints for bulk create/update/delete to reduce round trips.
rules.rationale: Batch operations improve performance for clients processing many items.

judge.prompt: Check if batch operations are supported for bulk operations
failCriteria: No batch support for high-volume operations

rules.title: Limit batch size
rules.description: Batch operations SHOULD limit the number of items per request (typically 100-1000).
rules.rationale: Unbounded batches can cause timeouts and memory issues.

judge.prompt: Check if batch operations have size limits

good: Batch limited to 100 operations per request

rules.title: Return individual batch results
rules.description: Batch responses SHOULD include success/failure status for each item, allowing partial success.
rules.rationale: Clients need to know which operations succeeded and which failed.

judge.prompt: Check if batch responses include individual operation results

rules.title: Use CloudEvents format for events
rules.description: Webhook payloads SHOULD follow CloudEvents specification for interoperability.
rules.rationale: CloudEvents is a CNCF standard that enables consistent event handling across systems.

judge.prompt: Check if webhook payloads follow CloudEvents format
passCriteria: Events have specversion, type, source, id fields
partialCriteria: Event structure exists but not CloudEvents

rules.title: Include event metadata
rules.description: Events MUST include id, type, timestamp, and source fields.
rules.rationale: Event metadata enables idempotent processing, debugging, and event routing.

judge.prompt: Check if events include required metadata (id, type, timestamp, source)

rules.title: Sign webhook payloads
rules.description: Webhooks MUST include signature header for payload verification (e.g., X-Signature-256).
rules.rationale: Signatures prevent webhook forgery and ensure payload integrity.

judge.prompt: Check if webhooks include signature header for verification
failCriteria: No way to verify payload authenticity

rules.title: Use POST for custom actions
rules.description: Non-CRUD actions MUST use POST with action name in path segment.
rules.rationale: POST with action name clearly indicates a non-idempotent operation that isn't standard CRUD.

judge.prompt: Check if non-CRUD actions use POST with action name in path
passCriteria: Action name is in URL path
failCriteria: Actions use GET with side effects

rules.title: Use clear action verbs
rules.description: Action endpoints SHOULD use clear verbs (cancel, approve, submit, archive, publish).
rules.rationale: Clear verbs make the action's intent obvious without reading documentation.

judge.prompt: Check if action endpoints use clear verb names
passCriteria: Names are clear: cancel, approve, submit, publish

rules.title: Include rate limit headers
rules.description: APIs MUST include rate limit headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
rules.rationale: Rate limit headers help clients implement proper backoff and avoid hitting limits.
rules.source: IETF Draft RateLimit Headers, GitHub API

judge.prompt: Check if rate limit headers are documented (X-RateLimit-*)

rules.title: Include Retry-After on 429
rules.description: 429 Too Many Requests responses MUST include Retry-After header.
rules.rationale: Retry-After tells clients exactly when they can retry, preventing thundering herd.

judge.prompt: Check if 429 responses include Retry-After header

rules.title: Document rate limit tiers
rules.description: Rate limits SHOULD be documented with clear tiers (per-second, per-minute, per-day limits).
rules.rationale: Clear documentation helps clients plan their request patterns.

judge.prompt: Check if rate limit tiers are documented
partialCriteria: Rate limits mentioned but not detailed

rules.title: Avoid breaking changes
rules.description: Do not make breaking changes within an API version. Breaking changes require a new major version.
rules.rationale: Breaking changes disrupt existing clients. Plan for evolution from the start.

judge.prompt: Check that API changes are backward compatible
failCriteria: Required fields added to existing schemas

good: v1.1.0 adds optional 'nickname' field - backward compatible

rules.title: Make additive changes only
rules.description: Only make additive changes: new endpoints, new optional fields, new enum values at the end.
rules.rationale: Additive changes are backward compatible. Clients ignore unknown fields.

judge.prompt: Check if changes are additive only (no removed or renamed fields)

rules.title: Ignore unknown fields
rules.description: Clients SHOULD ignore unknown fields. Servers SHOULD accept requests with unknown fields.
rules.rationale: Ignoring unknown fields enables forward compatibility as APIs evolve.

judge.prompt: Check if API tolerates unknown fields
passCriteria: No additionalProperties: false blocking unknown fields

rules.title: Use Deprecation header
rules.description: Deprecated endpoints MUST include Deprecation header with deprecation date.
rules.rationale: Deprecation header provides machine-readable deprecation notice.

judge.prompt: Check if deprecated endpoints include Deprecation header

rules.title: Use Sunset header
rules.description: Deprecated endpoints MUST include Sunset header indicating when the endpoint will be removed.
rules.rationale: Sunset header gives clients a clear deadline to migrate.

judge.prompt: Check if deprecated endpoints include Sunset header

rules.title: Document migration path
rules.description: Deprecated endpoints SHOULD include Link header pointing to replacement endpoint or migration guide.
rules.rationale: Clear migration guidance helps clients update efficiently.

judge.prompt: Check if deprecated endpoints document migration path
partialCriteria: Deprecation notice but no migration path

rules.title: Use consistent enum naming
rules.description: Enum values SHOULD use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants. Enum names should be singular nouns.
rules.rationale: Consistent enum naming improves readability and matches conventions in most programming languages.
rules.source: Google API Design Guide, Zalando Z-125

judge.prompt: Check if enum values use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE naming convention
failCriteria: Enum values use camelCase or lowercase

rules.title: Avoid abbreviations in names
rules.description: Avoid abbreviations unless universally understood (id, url, http). Use full words for clarity.
rules.rationale: Abbreviations reduce readability and can be ambiguous. 'cnt' could mean count or content.

judge.prompt: Check if property and resource names avoid unnecessary abbreviations
passCriteria: Only common abbreviations (id, url, http) used

rules.title: Use boolean naming conventions
rules.description: Boolean properties SHOULD use is, has, can, should prefixes (e.g., isActive, hasChildren, canEdit).
rules.rationale: Prefixed booleans read naturally and make the property's type obvious without checking the schema.

judge.prompt: Check if boolean properties use is/has/can/should prefixes

rules.title: Provide complete API info
rules.description: API info MUST include title, version, description, and contact information.
rules.rationale: Complete metadata enables documentation generation and helps consumers find support.

good:
info:
  title: User API
  version: 1.0.0
  description: Manages users
  contact:
    email: api@example.com

judge.prompt: Check if API info section is complete with title, version, description, and contact

rules.title: Define servers with descriptions
rules.description: API SHOULD define server URLs with descriptions for each environment (production, staging, etc.).
rules.rationale: Server definitions enable tools and developers to easily switch environments.

judge.prompt: Check if servers are defined with proper URLs and descriptions

rules.title: No verbs in URL paths
rules.description: URL paths MUST NOT contain verbs. Use HTTP methods to express actions, not URL segments.
rules.rationale: RESTful URLs identify resources (nouns), not actions. Verbs belong in HTTP methods.

judge.prompt: Check if URL paths avoid verbs and use nouns for resources
passCriteria: Sub-resource actions use POST with noun
failCriteria: Paths contain verbs like create, get, delete

generate.prompt: Use nouns for URL paths, not verbs. Express actions via HTTP methods.

rules.title: Use camelCase for query parameters
rules.description: Query parameter names SHOULD use camelCase to match JSON property naming conventions.
rules.rationale: Consistent casing between query params and JSON properties reduces cognitive load.

judge.prompt: Check if query parameters use camelCase naming

rules.title: Include error code in Problem Details
rules.description: Error responses SHOULD include a machine-readable error code in addition to human-readable messages.
rules.rationale: Error codes enable programmatic error handling and internationalization of error messages.

judge.prompt: Check if error responses include machine-readable error codes

rules.title: Document validation error details
rules.description: Validation errors SHOULD include field-level details showing which fields failed and why.
rules.rationale: Field-level errors enable UIs to show inline validation messages.

judge.prompt: Check if validation errors include field-level details

rules.title: Document pagination parameters
rules.description: Pagination parameters (limit, cursor) MUST be documented with default values and maximum limits.
rules.rationale: Clear pagination documentation helps clients implement efficient data fetching.

good:
limit:
  description: Max items per page (default: 20, max: 100)
  schema:
    type: integer
    default: 20
    maximum: 100

judge.prompt: Check if pagination parameters document defaults and limits

rules.title: Use consistent collection property names
rules.description: Collection responses MUST use 'items' for the array property, not resource-specific names like 'users' or 'orders'.
rules.rationale: Consistent property names enable generic client code for pagination and collection handling.

judge.prompt: Check if all collection responses use 'items' as the array property name

rules.title: Use discriminator for polymorphic types
rules.description: oneOf and anyOf schemas MUST include a discriminator with propertyName. Without discriminators, SDK generators produce unusable interface{} or Object types.
rules.rationale: Discriminators enable SDK generators to create proper typed unions. Without them, Go generates interface{}, TypeScript generates unknown, making the SDK unusable.

good:
oneOf:
  - $ref: '#/components/schemas/Dog'
  - $ref: '#/components/schemas/Cat'
discriminator:
  propertyName: petType
  mapping:
    dog: '#/components/schemas/Dog'
    cat: '#/components/schemas/Cat'

enforcement.reason: JSONPath filter expressions not supported by parser

judge.prompt: Check if oneOf/anyOf schemas have discriminator with propertyName

rules.title: Use named schemas for request/response bodies
rules.description: Request and response bodies MUST reference named schemas from components/schemas. Inline schemas produce ugly generated type names like 'PostUsersRequest' or 'GetUsersResponse200'.
rules.rationale: Named schemas become clean type names in SDKs. Inline schemas get auto-generated names that are verbose and inconsistent across generators.

bad:
requestBody:
  content:
    application/json:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          name:
            type: string

enforcement.reason: JSONPath quoted keys with slashes and $ref not supported by parser

judge.prompt: Check if request/response bodies use $ref to named schemas instead of inline definitions
passCriteria: Request bodies use $ref to named schemas
Response bodies use $ref to named schemas
Schema names are descriptive (CreateUserRequest, User, Error)
failCriteria: Inline object schemas in request body
Inline object schemas in response body

rules.title: Require response schema for all responses
rules.description: All responses with bodies MUST have a schema defined. Responses without schemas generate empty or any types in SDKs.
rules.rationale: SDK generators need response schemas to generate return types. Missing schemas result in interface{} or untyped responses.

bad:
responses:
  200:
    description: Success
    # No schema defined

enforcement.reason: JSONPath quoted keys with slashes not supported by parser

judge.prompt: Check if all responses with content have schemas defined
passCriteria: All error responses have error schema
No responses with content but missing schema
failCriteria: Response has content but no schema

rules.title: Use explicit nullable for optional null values
rules.description: Properties that can be null MUST use 'nullable: true' (OpenAPI 3.0) or 'type: ["string", "null"]' (OpenAPI 3.1). This distinction affects pointer vs value types in Go.
rules.rationale: In Go, nullable fields become pointers (*string), non-nullable become values (string). Incorrect nullable handling causes nil pointer panics or incorrect serialization.

good: middleName:\n  type: string\n  nullable: true  # Go: *string
name:\n  type: string  # Go: string (required, never null)
bad: middleName:\n  type: string  # Ambiguous - is null valid?
# Relying on 'required' array alone for nullability

judge.prompt: Check if nullable properties explicitly use nullable: true or type array with null
passCriteria: Optional properties that accept null use nullable: true
Clear distinction between optional and nullable
failCriteria: Optional without nullable when null is valid

rules.title: Explicitly define additionalProperties
rules.description: Object schemas SHOULD explicitly set additionalProperties to false (strict) or a typed schema (map). Implicit additionalProperties: true causes map[string]interface{} in Go.
rules.rationale: ogen and other generators handle additionalProperties differently. Explicit false creates clean structs. Typed additionalProperties creates map[string]Type.

good:
User:
  type: object
  additionalProperties: false
  properties:
    id: ...

Metadata:
  type: object
  additionalProperties:
    type: string  # map[string]string in Go
bad:
User:
  type: object
  properties:
    id: ...
  # additionalProperties defaults to true → map[string]interface{}

judge.prompt: Check if object schemas explicitly define additionalProperties
passCriteria: Schemas explicitly set additionalProperties: false for strict objects

rules.title: Use consistent response envelope
rules.description: Consider using a consistent response envelope across all endpoints: {"data": ..., "meta": ...}. This enables generic SDK response handling and middleware.
rules.rationale: Stripe and other leading APIs use consistent envelopes. This enables generic error handling, pagination, and metadata extraction in SDKs.

judge.prompt: Check if API uses consistent response envelope structure
partialCriteria: Collections use envelope but singles don't

rules.title: Support expandable relations
rules.description: Consider supporting expandable relations via ?expand=customer,items query parameter. Returns full objects instead of IDs, reducing round trips.
rules.rationale: Stripe's expand pattern is widely adopted. It reduces N+1 queries and improves SDK usability by letting clients fetch related data in one call.

good: Response includes full customer object instead of just customerId
bad: Requiring separate calls to fetch each related resource

judge.prompt: Check if API supports expandable relations pattern
passCriteria: Related resources can be expanded inline
Default returns IDs, expand returns full objects
failCriteria: No expand support, requires multiple round trips

rules.title: Support idempotency keys for mutations
rules.description: POST, PUT, PATCH endpoints SHOULD accept Idempotency-Key header. Store and check keys server-side to enable safe retries.
rules.rationale: Idempotency keys enable safe retries for network failures. Critical for payment and order APIs. Stripe requires this for all mutations.

good:
POST /orders
Idempotency-Key: ord_req_123abc

Server returns cached response for duplicate key
bad: No idempotency mechanism for non-idempotent operations

judge.prompt: Check if mutation endpoints support Idempotency-Key header

rules.title: Use verb + resource operationId format
rules.description: operationId MUST follow verbResource format: listUsers, getUser, createUser, updateUser, deleteUser. This produces clean SDK method names.
rules.rationale: Consistent operationId naming produces consistent SDK method names. client.ListUsers(), client.GetUser(id) is intuitive. Random names create confusing APIs.

judge.prompt: Check if operationIds follow verb + resource naming pattern
passCriteria: operationIds start with standard verb (list, get, create, update, delete)

rules.title: Specify array item types
rules.description: Array properties MUST specify items type. Arrays without item types generate []interface{} in Go.
rules.rationale: SDK generators need item types to create typed slices. []User is usable, []interface{} requires type assertions everywhere.

good:
tags:
  type: array
  items:
    type: string
bad: tags:\n  type: array\n  # No items - generates []interface{}
data:\n  type: array  # What's in it?

enforcement.reason: JSONPath filter expressions not supported by parser

judge.prompt: Check if all array properties have items type defined
passCriteria: Nested arrays also have item types

rules.title: Use standard string formats
rules.description: Use standard OpenAPI string formats for semantic types: date-time, date, email, uri, uuid, byte, binary. SDK generators provide special handling for these.
rules.rationale: Standard formats get special types in SDKs: time.Time for date-time, url.URL for uri, uuid.UUID for uuid. Custom formats become plain strings.

good: createdAt:\n  type: string\n  format: date-time  # time.Time in Go
id:\n  type: string\n  format: uuid  # uuid.UUID in Go
email:\n  type: string\n  format: email  # validated string
bad: createdAt:\n  type: string  # Just string, no parsing
id:\n  type: string\n  format: custom-uuid  # Unknown format

judge.prompt: Check if semantic string properties use standard formats
passCriteria: Date/time fields use format: date-time or date
partialCriteria: Some fields have formats, others don't

rules.title: Handle circular references properly
rules.description: Circular schema references MUST use nullable or array to break the cycle. Direct circular refs cause infinite recursion in SDK generation.
rules.rationale: Go structs can't have direct circular references. Use pointers (nullable) or arrays to break cycles. ogen handles these correctly when marked.

good:
TreeNode:
  properties:
    children:
      type: array
      items:
        $ref: '#/components/schemas/TreeNode'  # Array breaks cycle

Employee:
  properties:
    manager:
      nullable: true
      $ref: '#/components/schemas/Employee'  # Nullable breaks cycle
bad:
Category:
  properties:
    parent:
      $ref: '#/components/schemas/Category'  # Direct cycle - stack overflow

judge.prompt: Check if circular schema references are properly handled
passCriteria: Circular refs use nullable or array

rules.title: Support header-based versioning
rules.description: Consider supporting API-Version or Accept header versioning in addition to URL versioning for more flexible version negotiation.
rules.rationale: Header versioning (like Stripe's Stripe-Version) allows gradual migration and version pinning per request. More flexible than URL-only versioning.

bad: Only URL versioning with no override option

judge.prompt: Check if API supports header-based versioning option
partialCriteria: URL versioning only but migration path exists

rules.title: Include tenant scope in URL path
rules.description: Multi-tenant APIs SHOULD include tenant identifier in the URL path (e.g., /tenants/{tenantId}/resources). This makes tenant context explicit and enables better caching, routing, and debugging.
rules.rationale: Explicit tenant in URL provides: (1) Cache-friendly URLs where tenant is part of cache key, (2) Infrastructure routing to tenant-specific deployments, (3) Clear audit logs showing tenant context, (4) SDK ergonomics with tenant.resources.list() patterns, (5) Cross-tenant admin operations with explicit IDs.
rules.source: Google Cloud API, Slack API, industry best practice

judge.prompt: Check if multi-tenant API includes tenant scope in URL path
passCriteria: Consistent tenant path position across endpoints
partialCriteria: Tenant in path for some endpoints but not all
Mixed tenant in path and query string
failCriteria: Tenant only derived from token with no URL context
Tenant ID in query string instead of path

rules.title: Support tilde alias for current tenant
rules.description: Support `~` (tilde) as an alias for the current tenant derived from the access token. This reduces URL verbosity for the common case while still allowing explicit tenant IDs for cross-tenant operations.
rules.rationale: The tilde alias (Google Cloud pattern) provides ergonomic URLs for the common case. Users don't need to know their tenant ID for typical operations. Explicit IDs remain available for admins and cross-tenant scenarios.

bad: GET /v1/tenants/me/users (me is for users, not tenants)

judge.prompt: Check if API supports tilde (~) alias for current tenant
passCriteria: ~ supported as alias for current tenant
failCriteria: Must always specify explicit tenant ID

rules.title: Validate tenant ID matches token scope
rules.description: The server MUST validate that the tenant ID in the URL path matches the tenant scope in the access token. Return 403 Forbidden if the token does not grant access to the requested tenant.
rules.rationale: Tenant isolation is a critical security boundary. Without validation, attackers could access other tenants by guessing IDs. The server must enforce that tokens only access authorized tenants.
rules.source: OWASP API Security, industry best practice

good: Token scoped to tenant_acme accessing /tenants/tenant_acme/users → 200 OK
Token scoped to tenant_acme accessing /tenants/tenant_other/users → 403 Forbidden
Admin token with cross-tenant scope accessing /tenants/tenant_other/users → 200 OK
bad: Any valid token can access any tenant ID in URL
Tenant validation only in application code, not API layer

judge.prompt: Check if API validates tenant ID in URL matches token scope
passCriteria: Tenant scope validated at API gateway or middleware
failCriteria: Any authenticated user can access any tenant

designPatterns.title: Cursor-Based Pagination
designPatterns.description: Scalable pagination using opaque cursors instead of page numbers.
designPatterns.when: Any endpoint returning collections that may grow large
designPatterns.implementation: Use base64-encoded cursors containing sort field values. Never expose database IDs directly.

designPatterns.title: RFC 9457 Problem Details
designPatterns.description: Standard error response format for HTTP APIs.
designPatterns.implementation: Return Content-Type: application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields.

examples.response:
{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient Funds",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Account balance is $10.00, but transaction requires $25.00",
  "instance": "/accounts/12345/transactions/67890"
}

designPatterns.title: Optimistic Locking with ETag
designPatterns.description: Prevent lost updates using ETag and If-Match headers.
designPatterns.when: Resources that may be updated concurrently
designPatterns.implementation: Include ETag in GET responses. Require If-Match on PUT/PATCH. Return 412 Precondition Failed on mismatch.

designPatterns.title: Idempotency Keys
designPatterns.description: Enable safe retries for non-idempotent operations.
designPatterns.when: POST requests that create resources or trigger side effects
designPatterns.implementation: Accept Idempotency-Key header. Store and check keys server-side. Return cached response for duplicate keys.

designPatterns.title: Bulk Operations
designPatterns.description: Process multiple resources in a single request.
designPatterns.when: Clients need to create/update/delete many resources efficiently
designPatterns.implementation: Accept array of operations. Return array of results with same order. Use 207 Multi-Status for mixed results.

designPatterns.title: Long-Running Operations (LRO)
designPatterns.description: Pattern for operations that take too long to complete synchronously.
designPatterns.when: Operations that may take more than a few seconds (file processing, complex calculations, external integrations)
designPatterns.implementation: Return 202 Accepted with Location header pointing to status endpoint. Client polls status endpoint until completion.

designPatterns.title: Webhook Events
designPatterns.description: Push event notifications to registered endpoints.
designPatterns.when: Clients need real-time notifications of changes without polling
designPatterns.implementation: Use CloudEvents format with signature header. Include event metadata (id, type, timestamp). Support retry with exponential backoff.

examples.webhook_payload:
POST https://client.example.com/webhooks HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/cloudevents+json
X-Signature-256: sha256=abc123...

{
  "specversion": "1.0",
  "type": "com.plexusone.order.created",
  "source": "/orders",
  "id": "evt_abc123",
  "time": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
  "data": {
    "orderId": "ord_xyz",
    "total": 99.99
  }
}

designPatterns.title: Rate Limiting
designPatterns.description: Protect APIs from excessive use with rate limits.
designPatterns.when: All production APIs to prevent abuse and ensure fair usage
designPatterns.implementation: Include rate limit headers in all responses. Return 429 with Retry-After when limit exceeded.

examples.rate_limited:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 60
X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1640000060

{"type": "https://api.example.com/problems/rate-limited", "title": "Rate Limit Exceeded", "status": 429, "detail": "You have exceeded the rate limit. Try again in 60 seconds."}

designPatterns.title: Deprecation Lifecycle
designPatterns.implementation: Add Deprecation and Sunset headers. Minimum 6 months notice. Provide migration documentation.

examples.deprecated_response:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Deprecation: Sun, 01 Jan 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Sunset: Sun, 01 Jul 2025 00:00:00 GMT
Link: </v2/users>; rel="successor-version"

designPatterns.title: Expandable Object Relations
designPatterns.description: Reduce round trips by expanding related objects inline via query parameter.
designPatterns.when: Resources reference other resources that clients often need together
designPatterns.implementation: Accept ?expand=relation1,relation2 query parameter. Return full objects instead of IDs for specified relations. Default to IDs only for performance.

designPatterns.title: Tenant-Scoped URL Pattern
designPatterns.description: Include tenant identifier in URL path with tilde alias support for current tenant.
designPatterns.when: Building multi-tenant SaaS APIs where resources belong to tenants/organizations/workspaces
designPatterns.implementation: Use /tenants/{tenantId}/... URL structure. Support ~ as alias for current tenant from token. Validate tenant ID matches token scope. Return 403 for cross-tenant access without proper scope.

examples.current_tenant: GET /v1/tenants/~/users → resolves ~ to tenant from token
examples.admin_cross_tenant: GET /v1/tenants/tenant_other/users → 200 OK (admin token with cross-tenant scope)

designPatterns.title: Discriminated Unions for Polymorphism
designPatterns.description: Use discriminator property for type-safe polymorphic schemas that generate clean SDK types.
designPatterns.when: A field can contain different object types (e.g., payment methods, event payloads)
designPatterns.implementation: Use oneOf with discriminator specifying propertyName and mapping. Each variant must include the discriminator property.

examples.schema:
PaymentMethod:
  oneOf:
    - $ref: '#/components/schemas/CardPayment'
    - $ref: '#/components/schemas/BankPayment'
  discriminator:
    propertyName: type
    mapping:
      card: '#/components/schemas/CardPayment'
      bank: '#/components/schemas/BankPayment'

CardPayment:
  type: object
  required: [type, cardNumber]
  properties:
    type:
      type: string
      enum: [card]
    cardNumber:
      type: string

glossary.definition: Design approach where the API specification is created before implementation
An opaque token passed in the Authorization header for authentication
CNCF specification for describing event data in a common way
An opaque string encoding pagination position, more scalable than offset
RFC 8594 header indicating when an endpoint was deprecated
Entity tag for caching and optimistic concurrency control
Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State - REST architectural constraint for discoverability
An operation that produces the same result regardless of how many times it's executed
HTTP header for conditional requests, enables optimistic concurrency control
Naming convention using lowercase words separated by hyphens: user-accounts
Async operation that returns 202 Accepted and provides status endpoint for polling
Specification format for describing REST APIs (formerly Swagger)
RFC 9457 standard format for HTTP API error responses
A domain object exposed through the API, identified by a URL
An isolated organizational unit in a multi-tenant system (also: organization, workspace, account)
Shorthand like ~ (tilde) that resolves to the current tenant from the access token
Security boundary ensuring one tenant cannot access another tenant's data
JSON Merge Patch - format for partial updates
Naming convention using lowercase words separated by underscores (e.g., user_id). PlexusOne uses camelCase instead.
RFC 8594 header indicating when an endpoint will be removed
Uniform Resource Identifier, the address of a resource
HTTP callback that pushes event data to a registered URL when something happens
OpenAPI property that identifies which schema variant applies in oneOf/anyOf unions
Go OpenAPI code generator that produces type-safe, idiomatic Go clients and servers
Pattern where related resources can be fetched inline via ?expand parameter
OpenAPI property indicating a field can be null, generates pointer types in Go
